parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Continence promotion in adults
blurb: Categorise urinary incontinence, assess it properly and start the NICE NG123 first-line treatments, so pads are never the plan.
question: Mrs Akande, 68, rushes to the toilet every hour and often leaks before she gets there. She drinks six cups of coffee a day and her daughter has bought her incontinence pads. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate first-line plan?

teach.body: Urinary incontinence is any involuntary leakage of urine. NICE NG123 (for women) asks the nurse to categorise it at the first assessment as stress, urgency (overactive bladder) or mixed, and to start treatment on that basis, directing mixed incontinence treatment at the predominant symptom. Plain English: find out WHY urine is leaking and treat that. Continence can often be restored or improved, so pads are a stopgap or a last resort, never the first answer.

teach.caption: NG123 recs 1.3.1, 1.4.4, 1.4.11. Overactive bladder (OAB) = urgency, with or without urgency incontinence.

items.label: before OAB medicine benefit may show

items: Overactive bladder: recommend a trial of caffeine reduction.
High or low fluid intake: consider advising a change towards a normal intake.
Stress or mixed: supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months (at least 8 contractions, 3 times a day); continue if it helps.
Urgency or mixed: bladder training for at least 6 weeks; if frequency is still troublesome, consider adding an OAB medicine.

teach.body: Before starting, explain the chance of success, common side effects, that dry mouth and constipation may show the medicine is working, that benefit may take at least 4 weeks, and that long-term effects of anticholinergics on cognition are uncertain. Consider coexisting conditions (poor bladder emptying, cognitive impairment, dementia) and total anticholinergic load. Do not offer immediate-release oxybutynin to older women at higher risk of sudden deterioration. Avoid desmopressin over 65 with cardiovascular disease or hypertension.

teach.text: Pads, hand-held urinals and toileting aids are NOT treatment. NICE: offer them only as a coping strategy pending treatment, as an adjunct, or long term after treatment options have been explored, with a review at least once a year. And a positive dipstick in a woman WITHOUT urinary symptoms is not a reason to give antibiotics without culture results.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Akande in the continence clinic
teach.body: Mrs Akande, 68, has urgency and frequency and leaks before reaching the toilet. Her dipstick is negative and she has no infection symptoms. The nurse categorises urgency incontinence, gives her a 3-day bladder diary covering a working day and a weekend, recommends a trial of caffeine reduction, and starts bladder training for at least 6 weeks. Pads are agreed as a short-term coping strategy while treatment starts, with a plan to review.

items: Categorise as stress, urgency or mixed at the first assessment; treat the predominant symptom.
Dipstick all women; bladder diary for at least 3 days; no routine pad tests.
Stress or mixed: supervised pelvic floor training for at least 3 months, 8 contractions 3 times a day.
Urgency or mixed: bladder training for at least 6 weeks; caffeine reduction in overactive bladder.
Pads are not treatment; long-term users need an annual review.

summary: You can now categorise urinary incontinence, carry out the NICE NG123 initial assessment and start the right first-line treatment. You can also counsel safely about overactive bladder medicines and keep containment products in their proper place.

A.q: Mrs Lowe, 52, leaks small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes or jogs. She has no urgency or frequency. How should her incontinence be categorised?
options: Urgency urinary incontinence
Stress urinary incontinence
Mixed urinary incontinence
Overflow incontinence
A.why: Leakage on effort or exertion, such as coughing, sneezing or jogging, without urgency is stress urinary incontinence (NG123 rec 1.3.1).

whyNot.0: Urgency incontinence is leakage with a sudden urge; she has none.
whyNot.2: Mixed incontinence needs both stress and urgency symptoms.
whyNot.3: Overflow is linked to incomplete emptying or retention, which she does not describe.

A.q: Mrs Akande, 68, has overactive bladder and drinks six cups of coffee a day. Which lifestyle advice does NICE NG123 recommend first?
options: Restrict all fluids to 1 litre a day
Stop drinking anything after 4 pm
Wear pads until she is assessed
Try reducing her caffeine intake
A.why: NG123 rec 1.4.1: recommend a trial of caffeine reduction to women with overactive bladder.

whyNot.0: NICE suggests modifying a high or low intake, not a fixed 1-litre restriction, which risks dehydration.
whyNot.1: A blanket evening fluid ban is not NICE advice.
whyNot.2: Pads are not treatment; lifestyle changes can start now.

A.q: Which investigation does NICE NG123 say should NOT be used in the routine assessment of urinary incontinence?
options: A pad test
A urine dipstick
A bladder diary
A digital pelvic floor check
A.why: NG123 rec 1.3.14: do not use pad tests in the routine assessment of women with urinary incontinence.

whyNot.1: NG123 rec 1.3.5: dipstick all women presenting with urinary incontinence.
whyNot.2: NG123 rec 1.3.13: use bladder diaries in the initial assessment.
whyNot.3: NG123 rec 1.3.4: digital assessment confirms pelvic floor contraction before supervised training.

B.q: Mrs Kemp, 61, has urinary incontinence and new burning and frequency on passing urine. Her dipstick is positive for both leucocytes and nitrites. What does NICE NG123 recommend?
options: Start antibiotics without sending a urine sample
Send an MSU and start antibiotics pending culture
Send an MSU and wait for culture before antibiotics
Repeat the dipstick in 48 hours before deciding
B.why: NG123 rec 1.3.6: with UTI symptoms and a dipstick positive for both leucocytes and nitrites, send a midstream urine for culture and sensitivities and prescribe antibiotics pending results.

whyNot.0: A midstream specimen should be sent for culture and sensitivities.
whyNot.2: Waiting is advised when there are NO symptoms; she has symptoms, so antibiotics start pending culture.
whyNot.3: Delaying treatment of a symptomatic infection is not recommended.

B.q: Mrs Brown, 84, lives with frailty and had delirium last month. She is prescribed immediate-release oxybutynin for overactive bladder. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it, as it has the lowest acquisition cost
Give it at night to reduce daytime side effects
Query it, as NICE advises against it for her
Give it and ask her to keep a bladder diary
B.why: NG123 rec 1.4.29: do not offer immediate-release oxybutynin to older women at higher risk of a sudden deterioration in physical or mental health. Her frailty and recent delirium put her in that group.

whyNot.0: Low cost guides the choice among suitable anticholinergics, but this one is advised against for her.
whyNot.1: Changing the timing does not remove the risk NICE highlights.
whyNot.3: Monitoring does not make an advised-against medicine appropriate.

B.q: Mrs Ford, 74, has recurrent urine infections and says her bladder never feels empty. NICE NG123 recommends measuring her post-void residual volume. Which method is preferred?
options: A bladder scan
An in-out catheter
A CT scan of the pelvis
A 24-hour pad test
B.why: NG123 recs 1.3.10–1.3.11: measure post-void residual by bladder scan or catheterisation, using a bladder scan in preference because it is more acceptable with fewer adverse events.

whyNot.1: Catheterisation can measure residual urine, but a bladder scan is preferred.
whyNot.2: NG123 rec 1.3.19: do not use imaging such as CT for routine assessment.
whyNot.3: Pad tests are not used routinely and do not measure residual volume.

C.q: Mrs Young, 70, has mixed urinary incontinence in which urgency is the main problem. She has completed 6 weeks of bladder training, but frequency is still troublesome. What does NICE NG123 suggest next?
options: Stop bladder training and refer for continence surgery
Consider adding an OAB medicine to bladder training
Switch her to supervised pelvic floor training instead
Provide pads as her long-term management from now
C.why: NG123 rec 1.4.12: if bladder training does not give satisfactory benefit, consider combining an overactive bladder medicine with bladder training when frequency is troublesome.

whyNot.0: Surgery targets stress incontinence; her problem is mainly urgency, and NICE suggests medicine plus training.
whyNot.2: Treatment is directed at the predominant symptom, urgency, so bladder training continues.
whyNot.3: Pads are for long-term use after treatment options have been explored.

C.q: Mrs Ross, 79, has urinary incontinence. On examination after she has passed urine, her bladder is still palpable. What is the most appropriate next step under NICE NG123?
options: Start bladder training for 6 weeks first
Advise caffeine reduction and review in 3 months
Consider referral to a specialist service
Supply pads and review her in a year
C.why: NG123 rec 1.3.20: a palpable bladder after voiding is an indication to consider referral to a specialist service; it suggests retention or voiding difficulty.

whyNot.0: Bladder training treats urgency; a palpable bladder after voiding needs specialist assessment.
whyNot.1: Lifestyle advice does not address possible retention.
whyNot.3: Pads would leave possible retention unassessed.

C.q: Mrs West, 88, has chronic urinary retention causing incontinence. She cannot manage intermittent self-catheterisation and has no carer who can. A long-term catheter is being discussed. What should the nurse explain?
options: A urethral catheter will make her fully continent again
Intermittent catheterisation by district nurses must be used instead
Catheters are not used for retention in women
A suprapubic catheter may cause fewer UTIs than urethral
C.why: NG123 recs 1.4.21–1.4.22: chronic retention in someone unable to manage intermittent self-catheterisation is an indication for a long-term catheter; consider a suprapubic catheter, which may have lower rates of symptomatic UTI, bypassing and urethral complications.

whyNot.0: NICE asks staff to explain that indwelling catheters may not result in continence.
whyNot.1: Intermittent catheterisation is offered when the woman or a carer can do it; she cannot.
whyNot.2: NICE supports catheterisation when persistent retention causes incontinence that cannot otherwise be corrected.

reteach.title: Find the leak's cause before choosing the fix
reteach.question: Why does the nurse ask 'when does it leak?' before anything else?

blocks.body: Leaking on a cough or a lift points to a weak pelvic floor: stress incontinence, treated with supervised pelvic floor training for at least 3 months. Leaking with a sudden urge points to an overactive bladder: urgency incontinence, treated with bladder training for at least 6 weeks and caffeine reduction. Both? Treat whichever is worse. A 3-day bladder diary makes the picture clear.

blocks.text: Buying pads is not a continence plan. NICE: pads are a coping strategy or adjunct, or long-term only after treatment options are explored.

explain.body: At the initial assessment, categorise incontinence as stress, mixed or urgency (overactive bladder), start treatment on that basis, and in mixed incontinence direct treatment at the predominant symptom.

test.q: Mrs Hart leaks both when she coughs and when she gets a sudden urge, but the urge leaks are far more frequent. How does NICE NG123 say treatment should be directed?
options: At the stress symptoms first
At both of the symptoms equally
At the predominant urgency symptoms
At the symptom that started earliest
test.why: NG123 rec 1.3.1: in mixed urinary incontinence, direct treatment towards the predominant symptom; here that is urgency.

whyNot.0: Stress symptoms are less troublesome for her; NICE targets the predominant symptom.
whyNot.1: NICE directs treatment at the predominant symptom, not equally.
whyNot.3: Order of onset is not the NICE rule.

explain.body: Dipstick every woman with urinary incontinence; use a bladder diary for at least 3 days covering usual activities; measure residual urine by bladder scan if voiding dysfunction or recurrent UTI; confirm pelvic floor contraction digitally before supervised training. No routine pad tests, imaging or cystoscopy.

test.q: Mrs Sharma, 66, is starting a bladder diary for her incontinence assessment. What does NICE NG123 advise?
options: Complete it for 1 day, on a typical weekday
Complete it for at least 3 days, on work and leisure days
Complete it for 2 days, recording each leak and its trigger in detail
Complete it for 7 days, starting after treatment has begun
test.why: NG123 rec 1.3.13: encourage a minimum of 3 days of the diary covering variations in usual activities, such as working and leisure days.

whyNot.0: One day is too short and misses variation between days.
whyNot.2: Two days is below the minimum, and a diary records more than leaks.
whyNot.3: The diary is part of the initial assessment, before treatment.

explain.body: Stress or mixed: supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months, at least 8 contractions 3 times a day. Urgency or mixed: bladder training for at least 6 weeks. Add caffeine reduction in overactive bladder, fluid adjustment if intake is high or low, and weight loss if BMI is over 30.

test.q: For how long does NICE NG123 recommend bladder training as first-line treatment for urgency incontinence?
options: At least 2 weeks
At least 4 weeks
At least 3 months
At least 6 weeks
test.why: NG123 rec 1.4.11: offer bladder training lasting a minimum of 6 weeks as first-line treatment for urgency or mixed urinary incontinence.

whyNot.1: Four weeks is the time an OAB medicine may take to show benefit.
whyNot.2: Three months is the minimum for supervised pelvic floor muscle training.

explain.body: Containment products are not treatment: use them as a coping strategy pending treatment, as an adjunct, or long term once treatment options are explored, with a review at least yearly (continence, skin, symptoms, alternatives, product use). For OAB medicines, counsel about side effects, the 4-week wait and cognitive uncertainty.

test.q: Mrs Ball's daughter asks the district nurse for a supply of pads because her mother has recently started leaking urine. What is the best response?
options: Assess the type and cause, using pads short term meanwhile
Supply pads, as they are the first-line treatment
Supply pads now and arrange her continence review in 12 months
Advise a urinary catheter to keep her dry
test.why: NG123 rec 1.4.16: containment products are not offered to treat incontinence; they are a coping strategy pending definitive treatment. Assessment comes first.

whyNot.1: NICE says containment products are not treatment.
whyNot.2: An annual review applies to long-term use after treatment options have been explored.
whyNot.3: Catheters are for persistent retention that cannot otherwise be corrected, not new incontinence.
